o: Explain what a client and a server do.
Compare advantages and drawbacks for particular organisations.
c: Clients ask for services; servers provide them. The two computers have different roles.
Peers can each share and request files without needing a dedicated central server.
Central permissions, user management and backups can help larger organisations; dedicated servers need investment.
A small group can share directly at low cost, but there is no central backup and files may be unavailable if the sharing device is switched off.

m.title: Managed school accounts
m.q: A secondary school needs user logins, shared files and backups. Explain TWO advantages of client–server networking. [4 marks]
st: The school needs controlled accounts and reliable shared files.
A central server can manage logins/permissions [1], making access control easier [1].
Files are backed up centrally [1], helping restore data after failure [1].
Two separate advantages, each supported by a consequence, gain four marks.

w: A small art group with four laptops shares files directly. Explain why peer-to-peer could be suitable. [4 marks]
It needs no dedicated server [1], keeping setup cheap [1]. Laptops share files directly [1], which is simple for a small group [1].
A health clinic stores confidential files. Explain two advantages of a managed client–server network. [4 marks]
Central permissions restrict access [1], supporting confidentiality [1]. Central backups [1] let records be restored after a failure [1].
A peer shares a file but switches off their computer. Explain one disadvantage of peer-to-peer and another related to security. [4 marks]
The resource becomes unavailable [1], interrupting other users [1]. Without central security management [1], controlling access consistently becomes harder [1].
wSteps: Link the small number of devices to setup costs.
Peers share directly and need no dedicated server [2].
Lower cost and straightforward small-group sharing follow [2].
It needs no dedicated server [1], keeping setup cheap [1]. Laptops share files directly [1], which is simple for a small group [1].
Pick security and recovery, not entertainment.
Central permissions and backups provide distinct features [2].
Permissions protect access; backups support recovery [2].
Central permissions restrict access [1], supporting confidentiality [1]. Central backups [1] let records be restored after a failure [1].
Files depend on peers being powered on [1]; management is decentralised [1].
Unavailable resources and inconsistent access control are impacts [2].
The resource becomes unavailable [1], interrupting other users [1]. Without central security management [1], controlling access consistently becomes harder [1].

k.q: Simulate a server checking a permission flag.
k.code:
permission = 1
if permission > 0 then
    print("Access granted")
else
    print("Access denied")
endif
p: Add print("Request complete") after the IF statement.
k.a:
At permission = 1: Access granted. At 0: Access denied.

Extended OCR ERL:
permission = 0
if permission > 0 then
    print("Access granted")
else
    print("Access denied")
endif
print("Request complete")

Outputs: Access denied; Request complete. This is a simulated permission check.

Compare client–server and peer-to-peer networking for a large school. [6 marks]

Source: Original J277-style practice, not an OCR past-paper original.

Client–server: central server provides services [1], enabling permissions [1] and central backups [1]. Peer-to-peer: devices share directly [1] with cheap setup [1], but central control and backups are harder or files may be unavailable when peers are off [1].

Why may more cores improve multitasking?

Compare a LAN and WAN for two schools in separate towns. [2 marks]
A LAN covers a single small area [1]; a WAN connects networks across larger geographical distances [1].
